passage.title: Reading Part 3 - Test 14
passage.text:
Ocean Plastic Pollution Crisis

Every year, approximately eight million metric tons of plastic waste enter the world's oceans, creating a crisis that threatens marine ecosystems, human health, and coastal economies. This staggering amount of pollution has accumulated over decades, forming massive garbage patches and contaminating even the most remote areas of the ocean. Scientists warn that without significant intervention, the amount of plastic in the ocean could triple by 2040, with devastating consequences for life on Earth.

Plastic pollution affects marine life in numerous devastating ways. Sea turtles mistake plastic bags for jellyfish and die from intestinal blockages. Seabirds feed plastic fragments to their chicks, leading to starvation despite full stomachs. Fish and other marine animals become entangled in fishing nets and plastic debris, suffering injury or death. Moreover, as plastic breaks down into smaller pieces called microplastics, it enters the food chain. These tiny particles have been found in fish, shellfish, and even table salt, meaning humans are now consuming plastic regularly.

The sources of ocean plastic are diverse and complex. Single-use plastics—bottles, bags, straws, and packaging—constitute a large portion of the problem. In many developing countries, inadequate waste management infrastructure means that plastic waste often ends up in rivers and eventually flows to the ocean. Fishing gear, including nets and lines, also contributes significantly to ocean pollution. Even well-meaning recycling efforts often fail, as much of the plastic collected for recycling is actually shipped to countries with poor waste management or simply burned, releasing toxic chemicals.

Addressing this crisis requires action at multiple levels. Individual behavior changes—such as reducing single-use plastic consumption, properly disposing of waste, and participating in beach cleanups—are important but insufficient on their own. Governments must implement stronger regulations, including bans on certain single-use plastics, extended producer responsibility programs that make manufacturers accountable for their products' end-of-life disposal, and investments in waste management infrastructure. Some countries have already taken bold steps: Rwanda banned plastic bags in 2008, and the European Union has prohibited several single-use plastic items.

Innovation offers additional hope. Scientists are developing new materials that biodegrade more readily than traditional plastics. Others are creating technologies to remove existing plastic from the ocean, though the scale of this challenge is enormous. Emerging chemical processes can break down certain plastics into their original components, allowing true recycling rather than the "downcycling" that currently occurs. Additionally, some companies are designing products and packaging systems that eliminate plastic entirely or make it easier to reuse and recycle.

However, technological and regulatory solutions alone cannot solve this problem. Consumer behavior and corporate practices must fundamentally change. Many companies continue to produce excessive plastic packaging despite growing awareness of its impact. Fast-moving consumer goods companies, in particular, bear responsibility for much of the single-use plastic waste. Pressure from consumers, investors, and advocacy groups can push these corporations toward more sustainable practices.

The ocean plastic crisis exemplifies the broader environmental challenges facing humanity. It demonstrates how individual actions accumulate into global problems and how solutions require cooperation across borders, sectors, and communities. While the scale of the challenge is daunting, the growing awareness and mobilization around this issue offer grounds for optimism. With sustained effort, innovation, and commitment from individuals, corporations, and governments, it is possible to reverse the tide of plastic pollution and protect our oceans for future generations.
